Thanks so much for your generosity of replying so promptly and thoroughly.
I can feel your genuine care and concern for your students, parents and
community.

Are you familiar with any literature or research that your policy is based
on? Everything we have found has overwhelmingly shown it tends to at best
have short term compliance, at the cost of student mental health,
performance, etc. not to mention that the international community
considers it a human rights violation.

I have no doubt parents, admin and teachers who genuinely want the best for
students believe this works, we've just found the data doesn't tend to
support it and often quite the opposite. We've helped hundreds of schools
transition to more data driven policies and everyone has been and would be
happy, at any time, to provide and in-kind grant to help provide trainings,
policy, curriculum, etc.

I just received this email from a Superintendent in Oklahoma this AM.

"I commend your work. I was an administrator for 25 years in Colorado and
never once needed to paddle a kid. Out here, I have found that while some
parents expect it, the same disciplinary approaches work much better than
hitting kids. "

Anyhow, I know we are values aligned in our desire to help kids and
communitites and I really am appreciative of your reply.

With Gratitude,
Anthony David Adams

Hi John,

Sorry for the slow answer on this one; it deserved a real reply rather than a quick one.

The Arkansas boards that have taken it out of policy mostly did it inside the same policy code you have, 4.39, with one sentence:

"The [District] School Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment by any employee of the District against any student."

That exact wording is on the books at Lincoln, Searcy, Gurdon, Lafayette County, White County Central and Pulaski County Special. Fourteen Arkansas districts prohibit it in writing altogether; the others word it their own way (Bentonville: "Corporal punishment is not an approved method of discipline." McGehee: "It is the policy of this district that corporal punishment shall not be administered."). Each one is on our Arkansas page with the district's own sentence and a link to the document: https://earthpilot.org/kids/state/AR/

On the percentages, you are right, and it is exactly why the record quotes each district's own written rule and never ranks anyone by counts. A district of 359 students with one incident will always look worse in a rate table than Little Rock, which is why we don't publish rate tables.

I've attached a short inservice deck built for Arkansas: what 6-18-503 and 6-17-112 actually say (the immunity only holds for "substantial compliance" with the written policy, and not at all for four categories of children since 2019), the state's own numbers (8,932 Arkansas students paddled in 2017-18, 2,596 last year, down 71 percent with no change in the law), what the research finds, and the one sentence. Use any of it with your board, or with the staff, however it helps.

If Omaha adopts the sentence, the district gets the Safe School recognition for 2026-27 and a press release it can send to the Harrison paper, and the entry turns green the same day. And if there is anything that would make it easier with the board or with the parents who expect it, tell me what it is and I'll build it.

Anthony

body:
Hello,

I'm writing to request public records from the Indiana Department of Education under the Indiana Access to Public Records Act, Ind. Code § 5-14-3.

I maintain a free public record of every school district's written policy on corporal punishment, quoted from the district's own documents, at earthpilot.org/kids. Rather than write to every district in Indiana individually, I'd like to ask the department once for what it already holds:

  1. A current list of Indiana school districts with, for each: the district's website, the name and email address of the superintendent, and the name and email address of the records custodian or public information officer.

  2. Any list, index or link collection the department maintains of district student handbooks, codes of conduct, or board policy manuals.

  3. Any data the department collects from districts on the use of corporal punishment: counts, incident reporting, or annual filings, for the most recent three years available.

  4. Any department guidance, model policy, training material or correspondence with districts regarding corporal punishment, restraint, or student discipline policy, for the last five years.

  5. Any record of districts that have notified the department of a change to their corporal punishment policy.

Electronic copies are fine and preferred — a spreadsheet or a link is perfect, and nothing needs to be printed. If any part of this is voluminous, I'd rather start with items 1 and 3 than have the whole request delayed, and I'm happy to narrow anything on a phone call.

If fees apply, please tell me the estimate before incurring them. If any part is withheld, please cite the specific exemption.

Thank you,
Anthony Adams
Safe Schools Project, a project of EarthPilot

body:
Hello,

I'm writing to request public records from the Georgia Department of Education under the Georgia Open Records Act, O.C.G.A. § 50-18-70.

I maintain a free public record of every school district's written policy on corporal punishment, quoted from the district's own documents, at earthpilot.org/kids. Rather than write to every district in Georgia individually, I'd like to ask the department once for what it already holds:

  1. A current list of Georgia school districts with, for each: the district's website, the name and email address of the superintendent, and the name and email address of the records custodian or public information officer.

  2. Any list, index or link collection the department maintains of district student handbooks, codes of conduct, or board policy manuals.

  3. Any data the department collects from districts on the use of corporal punishment: counts, incident reporting, or annual filings, for the most recent three years available.

  4. Any department guidance, model policy, training material or correspondence with districts regarding corporal punishment, restraint, or student discipline policy, for the last five years.

  5. Any record of districts that have notified the department of a change to their corporal punishment policy.

Electronic copies are fine and preferred — a spreadsheet or a link is perfect, and nothing needs to be printed. If any part of this is voluminous, I'd rather start with items 1 and 3 than have the whole request delayed, and I'm happy to narrow anything on a phone call.

If fees apply, please tell me the estimate before incurring them. If any part is withheld, please cite the specific exemption.

Thank you,
Anthony Adams
Safe Schools Project, a project of EarthPilot
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com
11662 Old Lake Road, North East, PA 16428 · (234) 516-2545

name: Pulaski County Special School District
subject: Pulaski County Special School District recognized as a Safe School for 2026-27
body:
Dear Superintendent Senn,

Congratulations. Pulaski County Special School District has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Arkansas can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing Pulaski County Special School District with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "The Pulaski County Special School Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment by any employee of the District against any student." (policy 4.39), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com

Congratulations. Savannah-Chatham County Public Schools has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Georgia can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing Savannah-Chatham County Public Schools with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "The Board of Education does not authorize principals, teachers or other employees of the system to administer corporal punishment (paddling) on any student as provided in O.C.G.A. 20-2-730 et. seq." (policy JD), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com

subject: MSD Lawrence Township recognized as a Safe School for 2026-27
body:
Dear Superintendent Smith,

Congratulations. MSD Lawrence Township has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Indiana can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing MSD Lawrence Township with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

(policy 5630), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Dear Superintendent Eid,

Congratulations. South Bend Community School Corp has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Indiana can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing South Bend Community School Corp with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "Corporal punishment shall not be permitted." (policy 5630), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com

name: Belle Plaine
subject: Belle Plaine recognized as a Safe School for 2026-27
body:
Hi Randal,

Congratulations, and thanks again for pointing us to where it lives on your site when we wrote earlier this fall. Belle Plaine has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Kansas can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing Belle Plaine with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "JDA Corporal Punishment​ JDA ​ Corporal punishment shall not be permitted in the school district." (policy as sent by the district), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project

name: Raymore-Peculiar R-II School District
subject: Raymore-Peculiar R-II School District recognized as a Safe School for 2026-27
body:
Hi Mike,

Congratulations, and thanks again for sending the link to the policy when we wrote earlier this fall. Raymore-Peculiar R-II School District has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Missouri can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing Raymore-Peculiar R-II School District with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "Prohibited No person employed by or volunteering for the School District shall administer or cause to be administered corporal punishment upon a student attending District schools." (policy as sent by the district), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com

name: Lawton Public Schools
subject: Re: Lawton Public Schools corporal punishment policy
body:
Hi Neal,

Congratulations, and thanks again for sending the link to the policy when we wrote earlier this fall. Lawton Public Schools has a written board policy that prohibits corporal punishment in every school it governs. Not every district in Oklahoma can say that, and in the 17 states where the practice is still legal, most cannot. We are recognizing Lawton Public Schools with a Safe School certificate for the 2026-27 school year.

It's attached as a print-ready PDF featuring your policy's own sentence, "Adams, I have confirmed with staff that the district does not practice corporal punishment." (policy as sent by the district), and a QR code to the district's entry in the public record at earthpilot.org/kids, where anyone can see the source.

Your policy stands with:

  - The American Academy of Pediatrics, which in 2023 called for corporal punishment to be abolished in all school settings in every state, and whose 2018 discipline guidance found all forms of it minimally effective in the short term and harmful over time.
  - The U.S. Secretary of Education, who wrote to every governor and state education chief in March 2023 asking them to end it.
  - The American Psychological Association, the ACLU, the NEA, the NAACP and more than 100 other organizations, in a 2016 open letter calling for an end to the practice in schools.
  - The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (2012), the National Association of School Psychologists (2021) and the National PTA, each on record against it.

What the research says, briefly: a 2022 meta-analysis of school corporal punishment specifically, across 21 studies and more than 67,000 children, found it associated with more aggressive and disruptive behavior, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. A 2019 study of young adults from the states where it was legal found that those who had received it in school had lower high school GPAs and more depressive symptoms. The 2016 review of 75 studies and 160,927 children found physical punishment linked to 13 of 17 outcomes studied, every one in the direction of harm.

Nationally, 19,851 public school students were struck as punishment in 2023-24, down from 106,055 a decade earlier. Districts like yours are why.

Two things you are welcome to do with this: hang it, and tell people. A sample press release is attached as a Word document, written so your office can send it to local media with one edit.

One more, if you are willing. We are collecting thirty-second selfie videos from superintendents, principals and teachers in districts that chose other approaches: what you do instead, what changed, or what you would tell a district that still paddles. No script, phone in hand. Send one at earthpilot.org/kids/video/ and we will put a real face to this.

With respect and thanks,

Anthony David Adams
Founder, EarthPilot · Safe Schools Project
earthpilot.org/kids · anthony@175g.com
notes: Safe School certificate 2026–27; board policy as sent by the district.
